newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's growth will be poor for three years-Fazio.
newsitem.headline: Italy's growth will be poor for three years-Fazio.

text.p: Italian gross domestic product growth will be unsatisfactory for the next three years even though there are already signs of economic recovery, Bank of Italy Governor Antonio Fazio said on Saturday.
Speaking at the central bank's annual assembly Fazio also said he agreed with the three-year rolling economic strategy, known as the DPEF, approved by the government on Friday.
Fazio said although the central government was gradually easing monetary policy he would not hesitate to tighten the reins if conditions required.
In an apparent reference to the government's reported plans to widen value added tax bands, Fazio said further significant tax increases could blunt Italy's competitive edge.
The economy was heading for one percent GDP growth in 1997 amid clear signs of recovery.
""Macroeconomic evaluations indicate unsatisfactory growth for the next three years, unfavourable prospects for jobs growth, a growing surplus in the balance of payments," said Fazio said.
Tne central bank's growth forecasts were based on the assumption that labour costs would remain stable and the public sector deficit to GDP ratio would be kept within three percent.
Fazio said monetary policy would be subordinated to the aim of keeping inflation below two percent next year.

"The regulation of money and credit, the gradual easing of restrictions will be consistent with this objective. This will express confidence in the non-inflationary recovery of the economy and will encourage it," he said.
Fazio also called on the government to keep up its efforts to rein in public spending but warned that he would not hesitate to tighten monetary policy at the first hint of a reawaking of inflation.
"We assume that the correction of public spending will continue with clear intent and that inflationary stimuli will not be injected into the economy," he added.
"In the presence of unfavourable developments we will not hesitate to halt our policy of reflation, in extreme cases to change its course," said Fazio.
Turning to fiscal policy, Fazio said the tax burden was already very high as a result of high public spending.

"It would be an error to try to correct the disequilibria (in public accounts) which still remain by acting in a significant way on (tax) revenues, in particularly those which influence the level of prices and costs," said Fazio.
"An erosion of competitiveness would result because of the further share of national resources that would be withdrawn from productive use," Fazio added.
The government, which announced on Friday that it would seek to cut 25 trillion lire from the public sector deficit in 1998, has also signalled that it plans to raise revenues by hiking VAT taxes.
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said on Friday that any increases in VAT would only have a one-off impact on prices and would not be inflationary. Rome newsroom +396-6782560
